title: For its first 13 divisions, a fruit-fly embryo's nuclei share one cell

cover.alt: A glowing, oval fruit-fly embryo seen through a microscope, its surface packed with hundreds of small pink dots.
cover.credit: Bruno C. Vellutini, Tomancak Lab · CC BY-SA 4.0

body: A fruit-fly egg is only about half a millimetre long, and it starts life in an unusual way. Its nucleus copies itself again and again, **13 times**, but the cytoplasm around the nuclei is not split up, so they all share one mass called a **syncytium**. Most nuclei move out to the surface after the eighth division. Only after the 13th, when some 5,000 to 6,000 have built up, do cell membranes slowly grow down between them and make separate cells. Then gastrulation begins, and the embryo starts folding into layers.

slides.alt: An oval embryo covered in glowing dots. Dark waves ripple across it as the dots divide and become smaller and more crowded, then grooves appear and the surface starts to fold.
slides.caption: Time-lapse of a living fruit-fly embryo, about two hours in 17 seconds: waves of division sweep over the glowing nuclei, which get smaller and denser, then the embryo begins to fold.
slides.credit: Bruno C. Vellutini, Tomancak Lab, MPI-CBG · CC BY-SA 4.0 · excerpt
slides.music: “Kalimba Relaxation Music” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.heading: From one nucleus to a folding embryo

steps.label: Most nuclei move to the surface

slides.label: nuclei sharing one cytoplasm before any membranes divide them
slides.text: Until then, no membranes separate them: almost the whole embryo is a single cell with thousands of nuclei.

slides.heading: The first cells to form
slides.text: There is one early exception. After the 10th division, a few nuclei at the rear end of the embryo are wrapped into cells of their own, the pole cells. They are set aside to become the fly's germ line, the cells that will one day make eggs or sperm.

slides.clue: One mass of cytoplasm holding many nuclei, like the early fly embryo
slides.detail: The fly embryo stays one until after its 13th nuclear division.
